Introduction Background Advancements in the fields of science, technology, and medicine have contributed largely to the growth of society over the last century. Thanks to these discoveries, all corners of the planet are connected both digitally and physically. Progress in the field of medicine has led to people living longer, fuller lives and a general increase in global population. Awareness of our world’s changing climate and the effects that has on local and global ecosystems has spurred great efforts to protect the environment. These discoveries along with many others have helped our world grow in a myriad of ways; however, certain efforts in agriculture, natural resource management, and ecosystem management have not scaled to accommodate this growth. Increasing prevalence and ease of dissemination of invasive plants and animals, diseases, and changing ecological conditions pose significant challenges to biodiversity, ecosystem health, and agricultural productivity. Moreover, as the world population grows, there are more people to feed and less viable farmland to produce food for them. Despite the increasing prevalence of these issues, methods for addressing and tracking them have stayed relatively the same for at least the last several decades. Current Situation Current Systems and Operation Most agricultural surveying for weeds and crop irregularities still employs a farm laborer visually scanning the area. Moreover, unless the affected area convers a major section of the field, a famer is likely to address the problem with a hand sprayer instead of a sprayer vehicle or crop-duster. Advancements have been made in automating tractors and combines in an effort to assist planting and harvest. These improvements don’t, however, address the issue of maximizing the yield of the land itself. While arial surveys run by entities like the National Forest Service can provide useful information on large outbreaks of invasive species, the most useful surveying and prevention comes from fieldwork and input from the local population. Land surveying for mapping and appraisal is still most commonly done on foot with the help of a theodolite (a tool that’s been around since the 16th century). Deficiencies and Opportunities Current methods of addressing invasive species prevention, land surveying, and agricultural crop management often rely on manual surveying, which is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and prone to human error. Furthermore, the dynamic nature of environmental conditions, such as temperature, humidity, and precipitation, exacerbates the difficulty in both traversing these areas to perform surveys and tracking conditions to inform predictions. Recent advancements in automation, remote sensing, and data analytics present opportunities to revolutionize the way invasive species, diseases, and severe ecological events are managed.
